sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the requirements for a valid HIPAA authorization, including its core elements, required statements, and when an authorization is needed.
- Describe the release-of-information (ROI) process from request intake through validation, secure transmission, and documentation.
- Apply identity verification and the minimum necessary standard when disclosing protected health information.
- Recognize patient privacy rights, including access, amendment, restriction, confidential communications, and the accounting of disclosures.
- Apply scope-of-practice boundaries by following policy and escalating uncertain, unusual, or legal release requests to a supervisor or privacy officer.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An authorization is like a signed permission slip: it is a written note from the patient that says exactly who may see their private health information and why.

### Question 2

Think of it like the school nurse sharing a note with your regular doctor or with the office that pays the bill — those everyday care tasks do not need a new permission slip, but using the note for advertising or handing it to a boss does.

### Question 3

This is like a permission slip that must say exactly which pages of your notebook can be copied — not just 'some papers.'

### Question 4

This part answers the question 'who is allowed to send out the information?' — like naming which teacher may share your report card.

### Question 5

This is like writing the exact name and address on an envelope — it tells you where the letter is allowed to go.

### Question 6

It is like a permission slip that must say WHY someone wants to look at your papers, so you can decide if that reason is okay.

### Question 7

Think of it like a permission slip with a deadline stamped on it — after that date, the slip no longer works.

### Question 8

Your permission slip only counts if YOU sign it and write the date — nobody else can sign it for you (unless they are legally allowed to act for you).

### Question 9

It is like a permission slip that says 'you can take this back in writing anytime you want, and here is how.'

### Question 10

A permission slip without an end date is incomplete — just like a ticket with no date can't be used.

### Question 11

Psychotherapy notes are like a counselor's private diary about therapy sessions — the rules say those need their own special permission before being shared.

### Question 12

Think of it like a school not being allowed to give your home address to a toy company for ads without your family's signed permission.

### Question 13

Selling someone's private health details is like a business selling your diary for money — the rules say that needs your signed permission first.

### Question 14

It is like taking back a permission slip in writing — the moment the office receives your note, they stop using the old slip.

### Question 15

It is like pulling back a permission slip after a letter has already been mailed — you can stop future letters, but you cannot un-mail the one already sent.

### Question 16

It is like a doctor being allowed to help you even if you do not sign an extra permission slip — your care should not be held hostage to signing it.

### Question 17

Seeing your own report card is a right you already have; a permission slip is only needed to send that report card to someone else.

### Question 18

A personal representative is like a trusted adult who is legally allowed to make decisions and sign papers for someone who cannot do it themselves.

### Question 19

Some permission slips are so sensitive that they must be on their own separate form and cannot be stapled together with others.

### Question 20

If a note asking for private papers looks strange, the smart move is to hand it to a trusted adult (a supervisor) instead of guessing.

### Question 21

A permission slip with an old date is like an expired ticket — it no longer works, and you need a fresh one.

### Question 22

Before opening the file cabinet, first make sure there is a signed permission slip that says you may share the papers.

### Question 23

Checking a permission slip is like a checklist: make sure every required blank is filled in before you accept it.

### Question 24

Before handing over someone's private papers, ask to see a photo ID — just like a librarian checks a card before lending a book.

### Question 25

It is not enough to know who someone is; you also need proof that they are allowed to make decisions for the patient — like showing a note from a judge.

### Question 26

If someone only needs your math grade, the school should copy just that page — not your whole report card.

### Question 27

The rule says the office has about a month (30 days) to gather your records, and it may take one extra month only if it tells you why.

### Question 28

Private information should travel in a locked box, not on a postcard — secure fax or encrypted email is the locked box.

### Question 29

After mailing a letter, you keep a note of what you sent, to whom, and when — the office does the same for released records.

### Question 30

Think of the accounting as a list of the unusual times your info was shared — but the everyday sharing for your own care and billing does not have to be on that list.

### Question 31

If the office needs more time, it can take one extra month — but only if it sends you a note explaining why and telling you when you will get the records.

### Question 32

The office can charge you what it actually costs to make the copies and mail them — like paying for paper and stamps — but it cannot charge extra just to make money.

### Question 33

If your records are stored on a computer, you can ask for them on a computer file — the office should give you a usable digital copy.

### Question 34

A subpoena is like an official court letter — it goes to the person in charge (the privacy officer or lawyer), not to be handled by guessing.

### Question 35

When one doctor needs your chart to help treat you, they can share it without a new permission slip — it is part of taking care of you.

### Question 36

Sharing your bill details with the company that pays the bill does not need a new permission slip — it is part of getting the bill paid.

### Question 37

A lawyer asking for your private papers needs your signed permission (or a proper court order), not just a phone call.

### Question 38

Being family does not automatically give someone a key to your health file — they need your signed permission.

### Question 39

Sending a fax is like mailing a letter — double-check the address (the fax number) and mark the envelope confidential.

### Question 40

Email is like a postcard unless it is sealed — encryption is the seal that keeps private health info from being read by the wrong person.

### Question 41

A permission slip has to be written down and signed — saying 'it's okay' on the phone is not enough.

### Question 42

If two kids in class share the same name, you check their birthdays to make sure you hand the right paper to the right one.

### Question 43

If someone needs one page, copying the whole book is over-sharing — you should copy only the page they need.

### Question 44

Just like the office staff only open the file drawers for their own job, each worker should only look at the patient papers they actually need.

### Question 45

It means: share only the smallest amount of private info needed to get the job done — no more.

### Question 46

When doctors are actually caring for you, they can share what they need to help you — the 'just the minimum' rule does not block your care.

### Question 47

If you personally signed a permission slip allowing a specific sharing, the office can share what the slip describes without the extra 'smallest amount' rule.

### Question 48

It is like keeping a secret by whispering and putting the paper in a folder instead of shouting it or taping it to the wall.

### Question 49

Like a librarian checking your card before handing over a book, the office checks your ID before handing over your records.

### Question 50

On the phone you cannot see an ID, so the office uses a secret-check or calls back the number it has on file to be sure it is really you.

### Question 51

If a stranger asks for someone's private papers, the safe answer is 'I need to check who you are first' — not 'here you go.'

### Question 52

If something looks fishy, you take it to the person in charge instead of guessing or arguing.

### Question 53

First prove who the person is, then prove they are allowed to have the papers — like checking a photo ID and then checking that the name is on the approved pickup list.

### Question 54

If a permission slip lists only your math test, the office should copy only the math test — not add your spelling test too.

### Question 55

Keeping a log like 'on Monday we mailed the test scores to the tutor, with your permission' is how the office remembers exactly what it sent.

### Question 56

You keep the signed permission slip in the file so you can prove later that you had permission to share the papers.

### Question 57

You can ask for a list of the times your info was shared going back six years — like asking a store for the last six years of your receipts.

### Question 58

The office keeps its important privacy paperwork for six years, like keeping school records in a safe folder for a set time.

### Question 59

An audit trail is like a sign-in sheet that shows who opened which folder and when, so problems can be found and fixed.

### Question 60

The NPP is like a rule sheet the office gives you that explains how it keeps your health info private and what rights you have.

### Question 61

You can ask the office to keep some info extra-private; sometimes it must say yes, and other times it can politely decline.

### Question 62

If you pay for something yourself and ask the office to keep it off the insurance bill, the office has to say yes.

### Question 63

You can ask the office to call a different number or use a different way to reach you so your health info stays private.

### Question 64

If you think your privacy was not protected, you can tell the office and also tell the government — and nobody is allowed to punish you for complaining.

### Question 65

Even after someone passes away, their private health information stays protected for 50 more years.

### Question 66

A business associate is like a hired helper company (for billing or shredding) that also has to follow the privacy rules because it touches your health info.

### Question 67

It is like the official folder of papers about you that the office uses to make decisions — and you have a right to see and fix that folder.

### Question 68

If your report card has a wrong grade, you can ask the school to fix it — patients can ask the office to fix mistakes in their health record.

### Question 69

If you are told you cannot see part of your own file, the office has to explain why in writing — the front desk should not just guess.

### Question 70

The office gives you its privacy rule sheet and asks you to sign that you got it — but if you do not want to sign, you can still be seen.

### Question 71

An 'incidental' leak is like a neighbor hearing your name called at the desk — it is small and unavoidable, unlike leaving your whole file out for everyone to read.

### Question 72

The office writes rules and trains everyone so each worker only opens the file drawers they need for their own job.

### Question 73

If your private info goes to the wrong person, the office has to tell you about it — hiding or ignoring the mistake is not allowed.

### Question 74

Release of information is like the office sending your private health papers to someone who has permission to get them.

### Question 75

The special permission slip (authorization) is only for unusual sharing outside your care and billing — everyday care does not need it.

### Question 76

A permission slip only makes sense if you can actually read and understand it — so it is written in clear, simple words.

### Question 77

The accounting is a list that says 'on this date, we shared this info with that person, for this reason' — each entry needs those details.

### Question 78

If someone cannot speak for themselves and a family member is helping, the care team can share just enough to help, when that is what is best for the patient.

### Question 79

If you want the office to send your records to someone you choose, you write down who and where, and sign it — then the office sends it there.

### Question 80

When talking about someone's private health info, step away from the crowd and keep the screen turned away — like whispering instead of announcing it.

### Question 81

If you are not sure the permission slip is real or complete, ask the person in charge before opening the file cabinet.

### Question 82

If you cannot sign a permission slip yourself, only the adult who is legally allowed to act for you (like a guardian) may sign it.

### Question 83

For requests from other people or companies, the office follows its own rulebook (and state rules) and answers as quickly as it can — there is no one-size-fits-all clock.

### Question 84

Getting rid of private papers means shredding them into confetti, not throwing them in a bin where anyone could read them.
